Written sources and how to use this chapter

This chapter combines the complementary strengths of five reviewed university courses. MIT supplies a finite-size deterministic proof; Stanford supplies selection correctness and group-size analysis; Carnegie Mellon supplies the probability and cost-model distinctions; Princeton supplies searching contracts and partition implementation; Berkeley's assigned text supplies duplicate-aware three-way selection. Exact reading scopes and rejected candidates are recorded in the source audit.

Read Sections 2–5 before using binary-search laboratories, and Sections 8–13 before using selection laboratories. The worked bank teaches derivations; the examination rules consolidate them. Neither an algorithm's successful demonstrations nor a finite question bank establishes correctness on every unseen examination question. The proofs apply to their stated contracts, and the audit distinguishes proof from finite testing.

Prerequisites are loop invariants, induction, elementary summation, logarithms, conditional expectation and comparison-based sorting. This chapter re-explains each tool at its point of use. Tree search, hashing, string matching and full priority-queue implementation belong to their own chapters; here they appear only when needed to compare search or top-k strategies.

Order, rank, duplicates and the output contract

A key determines order; a record also has an identity or payload. Two records can have equal keys without being the same record. Assume a consistent total order on keys. A comparator must be transitive and must treat equivalence consistently. IEEE NaN, changing keys, and inconsistent comparators break these assumptions unless a deliberate total-order policy is supplied.

Let the sorted keys, including repeated occurrences, be x(1)≤…≤x(n). The one-based k th order statistic is x(k), for 1≤k≤n. Its zero-based sorted-array index is k−1. A value v is a correct answer exactly when

|{x:x<v}|<k≤|{x:x≤v}|.

To prove this certificate, put all strictly smaller occurrences first, then all occurrences equal to v. Their occupied rank interval is from |L|+1 through |L|+|E|. This proof permits equal keys; the distinct-key shortcut “exactly k−1 smaller elements” does not. For [8,3,3,9,3,1], value 3 occupies ranks 2, 3 and 4. A stable choice of a specific record among those three requires an additional identity tie-breaker; key selection alone promises no stability.

For even length, “median” needs a definition. The lower median has rank ⌊(n+1)/2⌋ and the upper median has rank ⌈(n+1)/2⌉. A numerical statistical median averages the two middle values. It may not be an input key and is meaningless for keys supporting only order, such as filenames. For [2,5,8,40], these outputs are 5, 8 and 6.5. Always state the contract before deriving a recurrence or choosing an option.

Selection returns a value or a record; partition selection additionally arranges a selected index so that all earlier keys are no larger and all later keys are no smaller. The earlier and later regions need not be internally sorted. Full sorting solves all rank queries at once and is a stronger output requirement.

Linear searching and the information supplied by a test

Unsorted membership search inspects occurrences until it finds the target or exhausts the input. If exactly one matching occurrence is uniformly located among n positions, the expected number of equality tests is (n+1)/2. An unsuccessful query costs n. If success has probability p, and its conditional position is uniform, the expected cost is

pn+12+(1−p)n.

For arbitrary conditional position probabilities pi, the successful expected cost is ∑i=1nipi. If successful key frequencies are known, ordering records by decreasing frequency minimizes this cost: swapping adjacent probabilities pi<pi+1 changes their contribution by pi−pi+1<0. This is an exchange argument, not an assumption that the original data are uniformly random. Unsuccessful probability adds the same n term for every order.

An equality-only failure eliminates one candidate. An ordered comparison can eliminate a whole interval. This difference explains why a password lock that says only “wrong” cannot generally be searched by numerical bisection even if candidate passwords can be sorted. Sorting candidate names does not create comparison feedback from the lock.

A sentinel appends the target so that an inner loop need not check the end condition each time. It does not reduce the worst-case number of inspected keys asymptotically. It also requires writable extra space or saving and restoring an overwritten position, and a final check distinguishing a real occurrence from the sentinel.

The unsorted minimum needs n−1 comparisons: every nonminimum must lose a comparison establishing a smaller key. A scan achieves that bound. Likewise, an adversary can keep an unseen occurrence as a possible target or minimum, so general unsorted search/selection has a linear worst-case information requirement. This is a model-specific lower bound; a supplied index or bounded integer universe changes the available operations.

Equality-only search: one candidate per failure

An equality failure supplies no ordering direction; all other untested positions remain possible.

The equality fails; it does not justify eliminating either ordered half.

Binary search through a half-open boundary invariant

Sorted random-access arrays allow cheap elimination. We teach lower bound first because it handles membership, duplicates and insertion positions with one invariant. Define lb(x) as the first index with A[i]≥x, or n if none exists.

Maintain integer bounds 0≤lo≤hi≤n with all indices below lo known to satisfy A[i]<x and all indices at or above hi known to satisfy A[i]≥x. The unknown region is [lo,hi); the possible boundary lies in the inclusive index interval [lo,hi]. These two intervals are different objects.

def lower_bound(a, x):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        if a[mid] < x:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo

Initialization makes both known regions empty. If A[mid]<x, sortedness proves that every index at or below mid is too small, so moving lo to mid+1 preserves the invariant. Otherwise every index at or above mid is large enough, so hi=mid is valid. The integer measure hi−lo decreases strictly. At termination lo=hi; every earlier key is too small and every key from that position onward is large enough, which is exactly the lower-bound contract.

For [1,3,3,3,7,9,12,18] and target 3, the tested indices are 4, 2, 1 and 0; the returned index is 1. A membership routine must then test i < len(a) and a[i] == x. Accessing a[n] after a failed search is a separate boundary error, even if the search loop is correct.

For this loop, count one key predicate per iteration; do not silently count an equality check afterward as part of the same counter. Its exact worst-case predicate count for n≥1 is ⌊log2n⌋+1=⌈log2(n+1)⌉. The largest remaining length after an iteration is ⌊n/2⌋, so W(n)=1+W(⌊n/2⌋) with W(0)=0. Targets before the minimum attain that chain. An ordinary membership routine that exits on equality has different best-case and exact path counts.

Computing (lo+hi)//2 may overflow a fixed-width signed integer even when both bounds fit. lo+(hi-lo)//2 avoids that sum for nonnegative valid bounds. Python integers do not overflow this way, but the invariant is still useful when translating to C++ or Java.

Upper bounds, equal ranges and searching by answer

The upper bound is the first index with A[i]>x. Replace < x by <= x in the loop. The equal-occurrence interval is [lb(x),ub(x)), and its length is the frequency of x. The strict predecessor index is lb(x)−1; the strict successor index is ub(x). Check the corresponding range before accessing either one. A closed numeric range [u,v] contains ub(v)−lb(u) occurrences when u≤v.

Binary search actually needs a monotone Boolean predicate, not necessarily a stored array. For integer candidates [0,N) with false values followed by true values, find the first true candidate by using if predicate(mid): hi=mid; else: lo=mid+1. Returning N denotes “no true candidate.” Invariant: every discarded lower candidate is false, every discarded upper candidate is true. A predicate that returns true, false, true cannot support this elimination proof.

For example, a shipping capacity C is feasible if a greedy left-to-right packing of nonnegative item weights uses at most D days, with order preserved. Increasing capacity cannot increase the required days: every packing possible at C is still possible at a larger capacity. Hence the minimum feasible integer capacity can be searched between the maximum weight and the total weight. Each feasibility test costs Θ(n); the full cost is O(nlog(U−L+1)), not merely logarithmic. The greedy test minimizes days because it puts the longest feasible prefix into each day; an exchange of a shorter first-day prefix cannot let a later day start farther right.

If a first true index t exists but no upper bound is known, test 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on until a true candidate appears; then bisect the bracket. This costs O(log(t+1)) tests, including the doubling phase. Check index zero separately. If no true candidate exists, unrestricted doubling need not terminate; a finite cap, termination assumption or timeout belongs to the contract.

Real bisection maintains an interval bracketing a monotone crossing. After s exact halves its width is (b−a)/2s, so at most ⌈log2((b−a)/ε)⌉ halvings reach width ε. Floating-point stagnation can produce mid == lo or mid == hi; detect it. A small interval alone is not a bound on residual function error without assumptions on the function.

Search variants, representation costs and lower bounds

Exponential search is the unknown-bound method just described applied to a sorted sequence. Jump search probes block ends separated by b positions, then scans inside the first possible block. Its worst-case key probes are bounded by ⌈n/b⌉+b up to endpoint details. Treating b as a positive real gives a minimum near n, then nearby integers are checked. This tradeoff assumes direct access to block ends; counting only comparisons conceals pointer traversal in a linked list.

Interpolation search estimates position from numerical key values. For sorted numeric data with A[lo]<A[hi], an estimate is lo+⌊(x−A[lo])(hi−lo)/(A[hi]−A[lo])⌋. Clamp or reject out-of-range estimates and handle a zero denominator. Its familiar expected O(loglogn) behavior needs suitable distribution and independence assumptions. Highly skewed keys can make it advance one position per probe and cost Θ(n). Numerical arithmetic, rounding and overflow are extra requirements absent from pure comparison search.

A sorted singly linked list has no constant-time midpoint access. A boundary search retaining interval length and a left cursor can spend n/2+n/4+…=O(n) pointer steps despite only O(logn) key comparisons. Repeatedly restarting each midpoint traversal from the global head can cost Θ(nlogn) pointer steps on a rightward path. State whether the requested complexity counts comparisons, traversal, or all operations.

For locating one of n+1 insertion gaps through Boolean ordered tests, a decision tree needs at least ⌈log2(n+1)⌉ tests in its worst case: a depth- d binary tree has at most 2d leaves. This exact gap bound does not automatically apply to a primitive three-outcome comparison with equality, or to equality-only guessing. A lower bound must match the allowed observation and output contract.

For a distinct sorted array rotated at an unknown position, at least one half of an interval is sorted. Test whether the target lies in that half's key interval; keep it if so, otherwise keep the other half. Duplicate keys can make both ends and the midpoint equal, hiding the rotation and forcing a linear worst case. In a strictly bitonic array, comparing adjacent middle keys locates the peak, then binary-searching the increasing and decreasing sides solves membership in O(logn). Plateaus need an explicit policy and may destroy a naive strict-slope proof.

Minimum, maximum and tournament certificates

Scanning separately for minimum and maximum uses 2n−2 comparisons. Pairing improves this. First compare the two keys in each pair; only the smaller can update the minimum, and only the larger can update the maximum. For even n, initialize from the first pair (one comparison), then use three comparisons per remaining pair. For odd n, initialize both extrema from one unpaired key and use three per pair. For n≥2, the exact count is

⌈3n2⌉−2.

An adversary explains optimality on distinct-key inputs. Label a key fresh until its first comparison, then classify its remaining eligibility as maximum-only, minimum-only, or neither. When two fresh keys meet, the larger loses minimum eligibility and the smaller loses maximum eligibility, eliminating two candidacies. There can be at most ⌊n/2⌋ such comparisons because each consumes two fresh keys. In every other comparison the adversary can eliminate at most one new candidacy: a fresh key loses to a maximum-only key, beats a minimum-only key, or is placed above/below an ineligible key so that it retains one eligibility; two maximum-only keys eliminate one maximum candidate; two minimum-only keys eliminate one minimum candidate; a maximum-only key beats a minimum-only key without a new elimination. Ineligible keys are placed consistently between the surviving minimum and maximum classes. These outcomes can be extended to distinct numeric values satisfying all comparison results.

At termination, only the actual minimum and maximum retain their respective eligibility, so 2n−2 candidacies must have been removed. If C comparisons occurred, they remove at most C+⌊n/2⌋ candidacies. Thus C≥2n−2−⌊n/2⌋=⌈3n/2⌉−2, matching the paired algorithm. This counts key comparisons, not loop conditions.

To find the largest and second largest distinct-ranked records, organize a knockout tournament. Every loser has a witness larger than it. Only keys that lost directly to the champion can be second largest: a key losing elsewhere also has its defeater below the champion, so cannot be runner-up. The tournament uses n−1 comparisons, then finding the largest direct loser uses d−1, where d is the number of matches played by the champion. A balanced bracket with byes gives d≤⌈log2n⌉, hence at most n+⌈log2n⌉−2. For a power of two the champion plays exactly log2n matches. This is a worst-case bound; a champion with a bye can require fewer comparisons. Equal keys demand a distinction between the second occurrence and the second distinct value.

Knockout tournament and the champion’s direct losers

Attached tree edges connect each result to its two actual participants. Direct losers, not all losers, remain eligible for runner-up.

Every original record is an undefeated maximum candidate.

Three-way partitioning: a constructive correctness proof

Save a pivot value before exchanges. Maintain four regions in [lo,hi): keys less than the pivot in [lo,lt); equal keys in [lt,i); unknown keys in [i,gt); and greater keys in [gt,hi). Initially lt=i=lo and gt=hi.

def partition3(a, lo, hi, pivot):
    lt = i = lo
    gt = hi
    while i < gt:
        if a[i] < pivot:
            a[lt], a[i] = a[i], a[lt]
            lt += 1
            i += 1
        elif a[i] > pivot:
            gt -= 1
            a[i], a[gt] = a[gt], a[i]
        else:
            i += 1
    return lt, gt

In the less case, the element previously at lt belongs to the equal region when lt<i; exchanging it with the unknown smaller key and incrementing both cursors preserves all three classified regions. If lt==i, the exchange is harmless. In the greater case, decreasing gt exposes a previously unknown key at that position. The exchange classifies the greater key on the right, but the replacement at i is still unknown. Therefore i must not increment. In the equal case, increasing i extends the equal region. Each branch decreases gt-i by exactly one, so there are exactly hi−lo classification iterations.

An iteration may execute two Boolean key comparisons (<, then >) rather than one abstract three-way comparator. Report the intended convention. A pivot copied from the range guarantees a nonempty equal block at completion. A pivot outside the input can give an empty equal block, so selection must not assume that such a value was found in the array.

Quickselect: keep one region and translate the rank

For a local one-based rank k, let l=|L| and e=|E| after partitioning. If k≤l, continue in L with the same rank. If l<k≤l+e, return the pivot value. Otherwise continue in G with rank k−l−e. The equal block, rather than one arbitrarily removed pivot record, determines the translation for repeated keys.

def select_value(a, k, choose_pivot):
    if not 1 <= k <= len(a):
        raise ValueError("rank must be in 1..n")
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)
    target = k - 1                 # fixed global array index
    while True:
        pivot = choose_pivot(a, lo, hi)
        lt, gt = partition3(a, lo, hi, pivot)
        if target < lt:
            hi = lt
        elif target >= gt:
            lo = gt
        else:
            return pivot

The implementation keeps a fixed global target index; the mathematical recursive explanation uses a local rank. They are equivalent because each rightward move accounts for the discarded lower positions in lo. Do not subtract discarded counts from target while also keeping global array indices.

Correctness follows by strong induction on the active length. Partitioning establishes the rank interval of the equal block. If the target lies outside it, exactly one strict region can contain the desired value, and the proper rank translation preserves the specification. Because the equal block contains at least the chosen pivot occurrence, any continuation is smaller. If all keys are equal, one partition finishes all possible rank queries on that input.

Correctness does not imply a good split. For distinct keys, always choosing the smallest pivot when seeking the maximum makes active lengths n,n−1,…,1. With one pivot comparison against every other key, the total is n(n−1)/2. Selecting the median on the same pivot policy still visits linearly many nearly full suffixes and has quadratic cost. Sorting recurses on both strict regions; selection follows only the region containing the rank.

Randomized selection: expectation without circular reasoning

Choose a uniformly random occurrence from the current range independently conditional on the previous history. For distinct keys, its sorted rank is uniform. For duplicates, assign an arbitrary fixed identity order inside each equal-key class solely for analysis. An occurrence in the central rank region has a pivot value whose strict sides are no larger than the bounds obtained from its identity rank; equal occurrences are removed together, which can only help.

For every active length m≥8, at least half the identity ranks lie between ⌈m/4⌉ and ⌊3m/4⌋+1. Any such pivot leaves either strict side with length at most 3m/4+1≤7m/8. Thus a “good” pivot has conditional probability at least 1/2 and shrinks the range by at least a fixed factor. The conservative 7/8 factor keeps rounding explicit; it is not a tight comparison constant.

In a phase starting with at most M elements, wait until the active size is at most 7M/8 or below eight. While the phase persists, a good pivot of the current active set finishes the phase, because its next size is at most 7M/8. If N is its number of partitions, conditional success probability at least 1/2 implies Pr(N>t)≤2−t and E[N]≤2. Each partition in that phase costs at most cM, so expected phase cost is at most 2cM. Summing phase sizes gives

E[T(n)]≤2cn∑j≥0(7/8)j+O(1)=16cn+O(1).

The first incomplete phase and the finite base range can be absorbed into a fixed constant. This proves expected O(n) work for every fixed input; a general linear lower bound gives Θ(n) for worst-input expected cost. The bound is conservative and does not equal the exact number of comparisons in a trace. It averages over the algorithm's random choices, not over a supposedly random input. A particular unlucky sequence can still cost Θ(n2).

It is invalid to replace E[T(X)] by T(E[X]) before proving linearity. For X equally likely to be 1 or 3 and T(x)=x2, these values are 5 and 4. Using a property one is trying to prove is circular. The phase proof bounds actual conditional work without that substitution.

For distinct keys and an abstract partition cost of exactly n−1 pivot comparisons, exact expected counts can instead be computed by conditioning on pivot rank:

C(n,k)=n−1+1n(∑r=1k−1C(n−r,k−r)+∑r=k+1nC(r−1,k)).

Set C(1,1)=0. If r<k, continue on the right; if r>k, continue on the left; if r=k, no child is visited. This recurrence supports small exact exam calculations. Its counter is different from the Boolean-comparison count in our three-way implementation.

Deterministic median-of-medians selection

The goal is a pivot guaranteed to discard a constant fraction without first sorting the entire input. Divide the input into groups of at most five, sort each constant-size group, and take its lower median. Let g=⌈n/5⌉ and let M contain those g medians. Recursively select the lower median of M, using rank ⌊(g+1)/2⌋. Then partition the original input three ways and recursively select only the necessary strict side.

def deterministic_select(a, k):
    if not 1 <= k <= len(a):
        raise ValueError("rank must be in 1..n")
    if len(a) <= 140:
        return sorted(a)[k - 1]  # fixed-size base, asymptotically constant
    groups = [sorted(a[i:i+5]) for i in range(0, len(a), 5)]
    medians = [g[(len(g)-1)//2] for g in groups]
    p = deterministic_select(medians, (len(medians)+1)//2)
    less = [x for x in a if x < p]
    equal = [x for x in a if x == p]
    greater = [x for x in a if x > p]
    if k <= len(less):
        return deterministic_select(less, k)
    if k <= len(less) + len(equal):
        return p
    return deterministic_select(greater, k-len(less)-len(equal))

This readable version allocates lists. Linear time is not a claim of constant auxiliary space: the live input/group/partition arrays can occupy O(n) total additional space and recursion depth is O(logn). An in-place implementation needs explicit group storage and partition management. A small lab may use a lower base threshold for demonstration; that is a different executable trace, not the finite proof's implementation.

Why the pivot discards enough elements

At least ⌊g/2⌋ medians are no smaller than the lower median p, and at least that many are no larger. Every qualifying full five-element group certifies three keys on its corresponding weak side of p. To get one convenient symmetric bound, discard a possible partial group and the pivot-containing group. Each weak side still has at least

3(⌈n/10⌉−2)

certified occurrences, with a negative small- n expression interpreted as the trivial bound zero. For distinct keys the retained groups certify strict sides. For duplicates, weak-side certificates suffice: the strict greater side excludes every occurrence certified ≤p, and the strict less side excludes every occurrence certified ≥p. Therefore either selected strict child has size at most 7n/10+6. Do not count three disjoint groups merely because three medians have been compared: each certificate comes from a separate original group.

For an ideal complete-group illustration, medians of [1,2,3,10,11], [4,5,6,12,13], and [7,8,9,14,15] are 3, 6 and 9, so p=6. The global median is 8. The approximate pivot is useful even though it is not the exact median. In the model, the separate representative row is a copied list of median keys; the original records remain in their columns. Purple identifies the chosen pivot value, while green and blue identify actual smaller and greater occurrences after pivot selection.

Step 1 of 7

The recurrence, including the work of choosing the pivot

There are two recursive computations: selection in the median array and selection in at most one strict partition. Sorting fixed-size groups and partitioning cost at most an for a constant a. Thus

T(n)≤T(⌈n/5⌉)+T(⌊7n/10+6⌋)+an.

The ordinary equal-size Master theorem does not apply to two unequal child sizes. For n>140, their summed upper bound is at most 0.9n+7≤0.95n. Choose c≥20a and large enough that T(t)≤ct for every integer 1≤t≤140. Strong induction gives T(n)≤c(0.9n+7)+an≤cn. The finite base is what justifies the ceiling and additive constant. Dropping them in a formal proof without a threshold leaves a gap.

The familiar ideal recurrence has child fractions summing to 1/5+7/10=9/10. Its level costs form an(1+0.9+0.92+…). This is useful intuition, but the finite induction is the precise argument. Selection has a comparison-model Ω(n) worst-case lower bound, so the deterministic algorithm is asymptotically optimal for a single rank. That statement concerns order of growth; it does not claim the smallest possible exact constant.

General group sizes and recurrence traps

Let an odd fixed group size be b=2t+1. A full group contributes t+1 certified keys when its median lies on the corresponding weak side. Ignoring only additive boundary terms, the discard fraction is (b+1)/(4b) and the selected child fraction is (3b−1)/(4b). The ideal recurrence is

T(n)≤T(n/b)+T(((3b−1)/(4b))n)+O(n).

The sum of fractions is 3(b+1)/(4b). It is below one exactly when b>3. Hence every fixed odd b≥5 gives the same linear asymptotic upper bound, with different constants. For groups of seven, the second fraction is 5/7 and the sum is 6/7; with ideal toll exactly n, linear substitution needs c≥7. For groups of five it needs c≥10. Real implementations also have group-sorting cost and finite boundary effects.

Groups of three give the bound T(n)≤T(n/3)+T(2n/3)+O(n), which yields an O(nlogn) upper bound. The equality recurrence with a positive linear toll is Θ(nlogn). This does not by itself prove that every implementation of the selection algorithm attains both worst child sizes recursively on a single adversarial input. Distinguish analysis of a recurrence from a matching algorithmic lower bound.

A repeated grouping technique illustrates how the same group size can lead to a different guarantee. Take medians of triples, then medians of triples of those medians. The second-level representative certifies four original occurrences on either side. Select the median among about n/9 representatives; approximately half contribute, so roughly 2n/9 originals are certified on either side. The resulting ideal bound is T(n/9)+T(7n/9)+O(n), with fraction sum 8/9<1. It is linear after boundary constants are handled. “Groups of three cannot support linear selection” is therefore an overstatement about one particular construction.

Selection from two sorted arrays

Let arrays A and B have lengths m and n, with m≤n. To obtain one-based rank k in their multiset union, put exactly k elements on the combined left side. Choose i from A and j=k−i from B, with

max(0,k−n)≤i≤min(k,m).

Define the left and right boundary keys using conceptual sentinels −∞ and +∞ for empty sides. A valid cut satisfies AL≤BR and BL≤AR. Both arrays are internally sorted, so these cross inequalities imply that every combined left key is no larger than every combined right key. The desired value is max(AL,BL).

If AL>BR, too many large A keys are on the left; decrease i. If BL>AR, too few A keys are on the left; increase i. As i increases, AL cannot decrease while BR cannot increase, establishing the elimination direction. Equal keys are allowed by the weak inequalities. Empty arrays work if the rank is valid; both empty arrays have no valid rank.

def kth_two_sorted(a, b, k):
    if len(a) > len(b):
        return kth_two_sorted(b, a, k)
    if not 1 <= k <= len(a) + len(b):
        raise ValueError("rank outside union")
    lo, hi = max(0, k-len(b)), min(k, len(a))
    while lo <= hi:
        i = (lo + hi) // 2
        j = k - i
        al = a[i-1] if i else float('-inf')
        ar = a[i] if i < len(a) else float('inf')
        bl = b[j-1] if j else float('-inf')
        br = b[j] if j < len(b) else float('inf')
        if al > br:
            hi = i - 1
        elif bl > ar:
            lo = i + 1
        else:
            return max(al, bl)

This numeric code uses infinities; for general comparable records, represent missing boundaries symbolically rather than mixing incomparable sentinel objects with records. Its cost is O(log(m+1)) boundary iterations with constant-time access. If both arrays have equal length n, the lower median is the union's rank n. A comparison decision tree has at least 2n possible output locations realizable in suitable interleavings, so it needs Ω(logn) comparisons; this gives a tight asymptotic bound, not an exact optimal constant for the displayed implementation.

For an even-length numerical median, select ranks (m+n)/2 and (m+n)/2+1 or use both boundary values at one median cut. Do not average the two input medians: relative interleaving, not only the two middle keys, determines the union's median.

Two sorted arrays: feasible cross-boundary cuts

Green records form a left side of exactly k occurrences. The two cross inequalities certify that every left key is no larger than every right key.

The arrays remain fixed; only the feasible cut changes. A wrong cross inequality determines the search direction.

Top-k, rank intervals and multiple quantiles

To output the smallest k occurrences without sorting them, select the k th value v, retain every key smaller than v, and add enough equal occurrences to reach exactly k. This takes O(n+k) output-inclusive time. Taking all keys ≤v may output too many if the threshold is repeated. If the output must be sorted, sort just those k selected records, for total O(n+klogk) with deterministic selection.

For streaming top-k largest values, retain a min-heap of at most k records. Its root is the weakest retained record. A new record replaces the root only when it is better under the requested tie policy. The total is O(nlog(k+1)) time and O(k) memory; sorting the final retained records adds O(klogk). This supports one pass and small space but is not the same cost as offline linear selection.

For a rank interval [i,j], select its boundary values and output all strictly interior keys plus the appropriate boundary occurrences. With distinct keys, selecting rank i, filtering the greater side, then selecting the desired endpoint in that side is enough. With duplicates, use occurrence counts or a consistent identity tie-breaker so exactly j−i+1 records are output. Unsorted interval output costs O(n+j−i+1); sorted interval output adds the interval's sorting cost.

For q requested ranks, choose the middle requested rank, select it in linear time, then recurse only in the relevant left and right ranges. In one level, active ranges are disjoint, so their total size is at most n. The tree over requested ranks has O(log(q+1)) levels, yielding O(nlog(q+1)) time. A shared equal block answers all requested ranks it covers. Asking for all distinct input ranks recovers sorted order and the comparison sorting lower bound Ω(nlogn). A single rank does not have n! distinguishable output permutations.

Weighted medians and absolute-error minimization

Each key xi may have a nonnegative weight wi, with positive total weight W. A weighted median has total weight strictly below it at most W/2 and strictly above it at most W/2. Equal-key occurrences must have their weights aggregated when testing a threshold. The lower weighted median is the first sorted key whose cumulative weight reaches W/2. For an exact-half gap, multiple real minimizers exist, and this convention chooses its lower endpoint.

Consider F(y)=∑iwi|y−xi|. Between adjacent distinct keys, increasing y by a small δ changes F by δ(Wleft−Wright). To the left of a weighted median this slope is nonpositive; to its right it is nonnegative. At a key, the subgradient spans the contribution of its equality mass, so zero belongs to that interval exactly when both strict-side masses are at most half the total. Thus weighted medians minimize weighted absolute deviation. If exactly half the weight is on each side of a gap, the slope in the gap is zero and every point there minimizes F. The mean instead minimizes squared error, so substituting it changes the objective.

Linear weighted selection can use a cardinality-balanced deterministic pivot while computing weight sums during partition. Maintain a fixed threshold W/2 and the discarded-lower mass, or equivalently a local remaining threshold. If the threshold lies inside the pivot's cumulative mass interval, return it; otherwise keep one strict region and update the mass offset. The pivot need not bisect weight: balancing record count still bounds the running time because only one count-balanced region survives. Using the unweighted median directly as the final weighted answer is incorrect.

def lower_weighted_median(records):  # pairs (key, nonnegative weight)
    if not records or any(w < 0 for _, w in records):
        raise ValueError("nonempty data and nonnegative weights required")
    threshold2 = sum(w for _, w in records)  # twice the desired local mass
    if threshold2 <= 0:
        raise ValueError("total weight must be positive")
    active = list(records)
    while True:
        keys = [x for x, _ in active]
        p = deterministic_select(keys, (len(keys)+1)//2)
        lower = [(x, w) for x, w in active if x < p]
        equal = [(x, w) for x, w in active if x == p]
        higher = [(x, w) for x, w in active if x > p]
        wl = sum(w for _, w in lower)
        we = sum(w for _, w in equal)
        if threshold2 <= 2 * wl:
            active = lower
        elif threshold2 <= 2 * (wl + we):
            return p
        else:
            threshold2 -= 2 * (wl + we)
            active = higher

This version computes a true lower count median as pivot using the preceding worst-case linear selector. Each retained strict side has at most half the active occurrences, so the selector calls and partition scans form a geometric linear sum. The local threshold is kept in doubled-mass units, avoiding division and remaining exact for arbitrary-size Python integer weights. The equality case threshold2 == 2*wl continues left, preserving the lower weighted-median convention at an exact-half gap. Zero-weight records do not count toward the mass threshold. Exact rational weights also work with exact arithmetic; approximate floating-point weights require a deliberate policy near half-mass ties.

Weighted median: accumulate mass across equal keys

Bar widths represent weight, not occurrence count. The threshold is half the fixed total weight; equal-key mass is accumulated together.

The sorted display is a transparent cumulative-mass demonstration; it does not claim that sorting is needed by the linear weighted-selection algorithm.

Implementation obligations and adversarial cases

The mathematical specification is the interface. State whether inputs are mutated, whether returned output is sorted, whether ties are stable, and whether comparisons or total RAM work are counted. Never use a stale pointer to a pivot record that moves during exchanges; save the pivot key or maintain its identity deliberately. Iterative quickselect controls its main stack use, but a recursive pivot chooser still requires its own recursion analysis.

A logarithmic-depth stopping rule followed by sorting a large residual range does not by itself prove worst-case linear selection. The preceding unbalanced scans can already cost Θ(nlogn). A true worst-case linear hybrid needs a bounded cumulative work budget of Bn before switching to a proven linear fallback. Then prefix cost is at most Bn and fallback cost is O(n). Particular library implementations require inspection of their actual contracts; the word “introselect” alone does not identify a proof.

For bounded integer keys in [0,U), a histogram and cumulative count can answer a single rank in O(n+U) time and O(U) memory. This is not a contradiction of comparison lower bounds; direct addressing is an extra permitted operation. If U is huge or negative keys need shifting, the model and resource bounds change. A histogram loses original identities unless separate buckets or payload references are stored.

For sorted range sums, precompute P[0]=0 and P[i+1]=P[i]+wi. A closed key interval query finds l=lb(u) and r=ub(v), then returns P[r]−P[l]. The prefix construction costs O(n) after sorting; each query costs O(logn) plus constant arithmetic. Sorting anew before each query defeats this reuse.

Complete summary and method choice

Start with the output contract and the feedback model. Equality-only unsorted search has linear worst-case work. Sorted random-access boundary search has logarithmic key probes and precise insertion-gap semantics. Selection needs one order statistic, whereas sorting establishes every rank. A three-way partition handles ties through a complete equal interval, and only one strict region survives a single-rank query.

Random pivots give expected linear selection for any fixed input under the stated conditional-uniform choice; a unlucky run can be quadratic. Median-of-medians gives deterministic worst-case linear time by spending linear work to certify a sufficiently central pivot. Its recursive pivot selection must be included in the recurrence. Two already sorted arrays permit logarithmic rank selection because a feasible cut can be searched without scanning all records.

Use offline selection for one rank or an unsorted top-k output. Use selection followed by sorting only the retained records for sorted top-k. Use a bounded heap for streaming top-k when memory and a single pass matter. Use multiselection for several known ranks, and full sorting when essentially every ordered output is needed. For weighted absolute deviation, use cumulative weight, not occurrence rank, to identify the answer.

Worked mathematical, conceptual and examination problems

The authentic items preserve their original options and independently derived answers. Two are explicit revisits comparing sorting with selection, and one is a searching-information bridge. The remaining problems are original or independently reconstructed course tasks. Their stated comparison conventions are part of each question, and every solution explains the elimination or counting argument rather than just naming a complexity class.

Authentic searching bridge and sorting/selection revisits

Question 1. Worst-case search for an odd three-digit password

Authentic examination · checked English adaptation

MS CS 1405 · Q116 · PDF page 25. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

A combination lock has an unknown odd three-digit password whose digits are chosen from 1 through 9. Each trial takes two minutes. What is the maximum time required, in hours?

1.

12

2.

12.5

3.

13

4.

13.5

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Correct option: 4.

The first two digits each have nine choices. Oddness restricts only the final digit, which has five choices: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. Repetition is permitted because distinctness is not stated. Thus there are 9·9·5=405 candidate passwords. In the worst case the correct password is the last candidate tried, and the successful final trial also takes two minutes. The time is 405·2=810 minutes, or 810/60=13.5 hours, printed option 4. This is a finite worst-case search bridge problem, not a direct repeated-class pigeonhole question. The conclusion assumes a systematic search without repeated trials and no additional feedback eliminating candidates.

Question 2. Authentic revisit: descending recursive median sort

Authentic examination · checked English adaptation

Phd CE 1405 · Q9 · PDF page 3. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

For distinct keys, SplitSort chooses the median m, recursively applies itself to R={x:x>m} and L={x:x<m}, and returns SplitSort(R), m, SplitSort(L) concatenated in that order. What is the final output order?

1.

Descending up to the median, then ascending

2.

Approximately random

3.

Ascending

4.

Descending

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Correct option: 4.

Use strong induction on the number of keys. Empty and singleton arrays are already in descending order. Assume both smaller recursive outputs are descending. Every key in R is greater than m, and every key in L is smaller than m. Therefore concatenating the descending R output, then m, then the descending L output creates a fully descending array. The answer is printed option 4. The selected median affects balance, while the concatenation direction determines the output order. This algorithm sorts both children; it is not quickselect, which follows only the rank-containing child. Options 1 and 2 contradict the inductive block order, while option 3 would require reversing the concatenation direction.

Question 3. Authentic revisit: sample pivot guarantee for sorting

Authentic examination · checked English adaptation

MS CE 1405 · Q59 · PDF page 13. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

A quicksort variant sorts the first 2n+1 elements by insertion sort and chooses their median as pivot, then proceeds as ordinary quicksort. Which recurrence describes the worst case, suppressing rounding and constant terms?

1.
T(n)=2T(n−1)+n
2.
T(n)=2T(n)+n
3.
T(n)=2T(n−n)+n
4.
T(n)=T(n−n)+T(n)+n
Read the complete solution and reasoning

Correct option: 4.

  1. Sorting a sample of size Θ(n) by insertion sort costs Θ(n); partitioning also costs Θ(n).
  2. The sample median has at least n sample elements on each side. Thus neither partition can leave fewer than approximately n elements on its smaller side, but the rest of the array can all lie on the larger side.
  3. The worst split is therefore approximately n versus n−n, giving option 4.
  4. Options 1 and 3 duplicate a large branch and count more elements than the partition contains. Option 2 incorrectly treats the small sample as the whole input.

Transfer rule. Derive partition guarantees from the sample, and check that child sizes add to the parent size up to the pivot.

Selection contrast. This original question asks about quicksort, so both strict children are sorted. A single-rank selector would follow only one child and would need a separate recurrence. A sample median is not the global median and is not the median-of-medians construction.

Question 4. A repeated key occupies several ranks

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

For A=[8,3,3,9,3,1], determine every valid rank for the value 3. Explain why counting strictly smaller keys alone does not determine a unique rank.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

There is one key below 3 and four keys at most 3. The certificate is 1<k≤4, so ranks 2, 3 and 4 all return 3. Sorting yields [1,3,3,3,8,9], confirming the interval. Counting strictly smaller keys identifies the first occurrence rank, not every occupied rank. To select a particular record identity among equal keys, add a stated secondary ordering; it cannot be inferred from key comparisons alone.

Question 5. Lower, upper and numerical median

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

An array has keys [40,2,8,5]. Give its lower median, upper median and numerical median. Which answers remain defined if keys support only ordering?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The sorted keys are [2,5,8,40]. With n=4, lower rank is ⌊5/2⌋=2 and upper rank is ⌈5/2⌉=3, giving 5 and 8. Averaging gives 6.5. The first two require only key order and return actual keys. Averaging requires numerical addition and division and can produce a value absent from the input. Consequently a comparison-only selection contract must not silently replace the lower median by 6.5.

Question 6. A rank certificate without sorting

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

A 120-record array has 41 keys strictly below v and 28 keys equal to v. Which requested ranks can immediately return v? What local rank results if the request is 95 and the greater region is retained?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The equal block occupies ranks 42 through 69 because 41<k≤41+28. A request of 95 lies above it. Discarding both lower and equal occurrences leaves local rank 95−41−28=26 in a greater region of size 120−69=51. Subtracting only 42 would be wrong because it treats 28 equal occurrences as one pivot. The new rank is valid since 1≤26≤51.

Question 7. Partition selection does not sort its sides

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Is [2,1,3,9,7,8] a valid partition-selection result for rank 3? Is it a sorted result? Explain the two contracts.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Index 2 holds 3. Every earlier key is at most 3 and every later key is at least 3, so its order-statistic certificate is valid. The left pair [2,1] and the right region [9,7,8] are internally unsorted. Partition selection establishes only the cross-boundary order, whereas sorting establishes every pair's rank order. A later binary search over either unsorted region is therefore unjustified. The output may be sufficient for rank 3 while insufficient for arbitrary membership queries.

Question 8. The comparator can invalidate a proof

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

A programmer compares strings by length but declares equal-length distinct strings incomparable rather than equal. Which selection assumption needs repair? Give a suitable policy.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The partition proof requires every key to belong to exactly one of the less, equal and greater regions under a consistent total preorder. Length comparison can validly treat all equal lengths as equivalent, even if records differ. Alternatively compare (length, lexicographic string) to obtain a total order on string keys. Merely declaring neither less nor greater nor equivalent leaves records unclassified and invalidates the exhaustive partition. The policy should state whether the task selects a length class or a specific lexicographic record.

Question 9. Expected linear-search work with failures

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

There are 99 records. A query succeeds with probability 0.6, and conditional on success its unique position is uniform. Compute expected equality tests, including failures.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Conditional successful cost is (99+1)/2=50. An unsuccessful query inspects every record and costs 99. Total expectation is 0.6·50+0.4·99=69.6. The answer need not be an integer because it is an average. Using only 50 ignores failures; using 99 for every query ignores early success. This calculation assumes unique successful occurrences and uniform conditional position; repeated targets or unequal positional probabilities require a different distribution.

Question 10. Optimal scan order from frequencies

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Successful queries target four records with probabilities 0.1,0.4,0.2,0.3. Find the minimum expected successful scan cost and justify optimality.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Order the probabilities as 0.4,0.3,0.2,0.1. The expected number of tests is 1(0.4)+2(0.3)+3(0.2)+4(0.1)=2. If an adjacent pair is in increasing probability order, swapping it decreases expected cost by the difference of the two probabilities. Repeatedly removing such inversions yields decreasing probability order, so the exchange argument proves global optimality. This policy minimizes successful equality tests; it does not keep an independent numeric sorting invariant required by binary search.

Question 11. Equality feedback versus ordered feedback

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

There are 1024 candidate codes. Compare the worst-case trials needed to unlock by equality-only feedback with the Boolean questions needed merely to identify a hidden ordered code using threshold feedback.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

With only success or failure, each failure eliminates one candidate, and the last successful trial is still required to unlock. Worst case is 1024 trials. If merely identifying the code is enough, 1023 failed tests determine the last candidate without trying it. Threshold questions split the candidate interval; identifying one of 1024 possibilities takes 10 balanced Boolean questions because 210=1024. The feedback and terminal action differ, so applying the logarithmic identification bound to an actual equality-only lock is a contract error.

Question 12. Sentinel cost accounting

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

A failed linear search scans 20 original keys, followed by a sentinel equal to the target. How many equality checks occur? Does the sentinel improve asymptotic key-inspection cost?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The loop compares the target with 20 original keys and then with the sentinel, for 21 equality checks. A final position test distinguishes the sentinel from a true original match; it is an index comparison, not another key equality test. The sentinel removes repeated bounds checks inside the loop but does not turn a linear scan into a sublinear search. If the sentinel overwrites an original slot, saving, checking and restoring that key must also be included in the implementation contract.

Question 13. An adversarial unsorted minimum

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Why do n possible output identities not imply an O(logn) algorithm for the minimum of n unsorted distinct keys?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

An output-count decision-tree bound gives only the weaker lower bound ⌈log2n⌉. To certify a minimum, each of the other n−1 records must lose a comparison to a smaller record, directly or through a transitive chain. A single comparison can give at most one record its first loss, requiring n−1 comparisons. A scan meets that bound. Counting output labels alone overlooks the certificates required to distinguish them, so it need not be a tight lower bound.

Question 20. Midpoint overflow

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original; searching exercise pattern from Princeton §4.2

With signed 32-bit indices, let lo=1500000000 and hi=2000000000. Explain why (lo+hi)/2 is unsafe and compute a safe integer midpoint.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The sum is 3500000000, larger than the maximum signed 32-bit value 2147483647. Overflow may produce an invalid negative midpoint before division. The difference hi−lo=500000000 fits, so the safe expression gives 1500000000+250000000=1750000000. This argument assumes nonnegative valid array bounds; the difference itself needs checking for arbitrary signed endpoints. Python's unbounded integers avoid this specific overflow, but translated fixed-width code must preserve the valid arithmetic range.

Question 21. The unsorted-array counterexample

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original; searching exercise pattern from Princeton §4.2

Run lower bound for target 1 on [1,9,0]. Explain why inspecting only the searched positions cannot validate the entire sortedness precondition.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Midpoint 1 holds 9, so hi=1. Midpoint 0 holds 1, so hi=0, and boundary 0 happens to find the target. This lucky result is not a proof for unsorted input. For target 0 on the same array, the loop again returns 0 and a membership test incorrectly reports absence even though index 2 contains 0. The skipped region violates monotonicity. Checking only visited midpoint keys cannot reveal every hidden inversion. Validate a static array once, or maintain sortedness through updates; rechecking every query costs linear work.

Question 23. Binary search on shipping capacity

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Weights are [7,2,5,10,8] and at most two days are allowed, with order preserved. Find minimum feasible integer capacity and explain the feasibility test cost.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Capacity 18 packs [7,2,5] on day one and [10,8] on day two, so it is feasible. Capacity 17 packs [7,2,5], then [10], then [8], requiring three days. Feasibility is monotone, so 18 is minimal. A greedy test scans every item and starts a new day only when the next item would exceed capacity; its longest-prefix choice never wastes an opportunity to advance the starting position of later days. Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The probes are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128. Seven are false and the eighth is true. The first true index lies among integers 65 through 128 inclusive. A boundary search can use lo=65,hi=129 as an exclusive candidate range, or a false/true sentinel contract with bounds 64 and 128; do not mix their updates. The doubling phase and bisection together cost O(log70) tests. A finite upper bound or eventual truth is required for termination.

Question 25. Bisection accuracy is an interval claim

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

A real crossing is bracketed in an interval of width 10. How many exact halvings ensure width at most 10−3? Does this ensure the function residual is at most 10−3?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Require 10/2s≤0.001, so 2s≥10000. Since 213=8192 and 214=16384, fourteen halvings suffice and thirteen do not. The statement bounds the uncertainty in the argument, not automatically the function residual. A steep function can change substantially over a narrow interval, and a discontinuous function may have a crossing without a zero. A residual guarantee needs additional assumptions such as a Lipschitz bound or continuity plus a suitable stopping criterion.

Question 26. Jump-search block optimization

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

For 10000 records, use the simplified cost bound 10000/b+b for positive integer block size b. Find the minimizing integer and explain the model assumption.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The real derivative is −10000/b2+1, which vanishes at b=100. Equivalently, AM–GM gives 10000/b+b≥200, with equality at 100. This is also an integer and therefore minimizes this simplified bound. Actual ceilings and endpoint comparisons can change exact counts. Probing a block end is assumed to cost constant random access; a linked list requires following intervening links and does not get the same total-operation bound merely from the number of key probes.

Question 27. An interpolation-search adversary

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Let sorted keys be 0,1,2,…,n−2,n3. For target n−2, explain why straightforward interpolation can repeatedly advance by one position.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

With the huge right endpoint retained, the predicted offset is approximately (x−A[lo])(hi−lo)/(n3−A[lo]), which is below one for the ordinary low keys when n is sufficiently large. Flooring yields the left endpoint. After comparing that key, advancing lo by one can repeat this pattern until reaching the target. The distribution is highly skewed, so a uniform-distribution expected bound does not apply. Guarding progress prevents an infinite loop but still permits linear work; a binary fallback gives a different algorithm.

Question 28. Comparisons and pointer traversal differ

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Explain the total pointer cost of repeatedly restarting midpoint traversal at the head of a sorted singly linked list on a rightward binary-search path. Compare an interval-aware cursor implementation.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

On a path retaining the right side, midpoint positions relative to the global head stay near n/2,3n/4,7n/8,…. There are Θ(logn) such probes, each walking Θ(n) links from the head, for Θ(nlogn) pointer operations. An implementation that retains the current left cursor walks only roughly half the current interval at each stage: n/2+n/4+…=O(n). Both can use logarithmically many key comparisons. The requested computational model determines which statement answers the question.

Question 29. The insertion-gap lower bound

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

How many worst-case Boolean ordered tests are necessary to distinguish the insertion gap among 32 possible gaps? Explain why changing the primitive to equality-only feedback invalidates this conclusion as a tight achievable bound.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

A binary decision tree with depth d has at most 2d leaves. Thirty-two distinct gaps need d≥5, and balanced threshold tests attain five. Equality-only failure does not select a left or right interval; it eliminates only the guessed key. Consequently the same information-count bound remains a weak counting observation but does not show that five equality guesses suffice. A lower bound on leaf count and an algorithm exploiting ordered threshold observations are separate parts of an optimality argument.

Question 30. Rotated search with duplicate ambiguity

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original; pattern from Princeton §4.2

Why can searching a rotated sorted array with duplicate keys require linear worst-case work? Construct an indistinguishability example.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Consider length n arrays containing only 1 except possibly one 0. Each possible position of 0 can occur in a rotation of a sorted array. Searching for 0, any probed 1 provides no indication of which side contains the unique 0. An adversary places it at the last uninspected position, forcing n probes in the worst case. When endpoint and midpoint values all equal 1, the distinct-key sorted-half rule cannot identify a direction. Shrinking one endpoint is safe but may make only one-position progress.

Question 31. Bitonic peak and membership

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original; pattern from Princeton §4.2

For a strictly bitonic array, prove the peak-search direction using the comparison of A[mid] with A[mid+1]. Then give a membership algorithm and its cost.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

If A[mid]<A[mid+1], the pair lies on the strictly increasing side, so the peak is to the right of mid. Otherwise the pair is decreasing and the peak is at or left of mid. Maintain an inclusive peak interval with mid<hi, ensuring mid+1 exists. Each update halves the interval. Once the peak is known, search the increasing prefix with its ordinary order and the decreasing suffix with reversed inequalities. The three logarithmic searches total O(logn); strict bitonicity is needed for the simple slope argument.

Original

Read the complete solution and reasoning

For 20 records, compare the first pair once, then process nine remaining pairs at three comparisons each: 1+27=28. For 21 records, initialize minimum and maximum from the unpaired record with no key comparison, then process ten pairs: 30 comparisons. Both equal ⌈3n/2⌉−2. Counting two comparisons for initialization in the even case overcounts; treating the odd singleton as a pair undercounts or invents a nonexistent comparison. The tournament uses seven comparisons. The champion wins three matches, so exactly three opponents lost directly to it. Their maximum costs two more comparisons, for nine total. This transitive certificate reduces the candidate set from seven to three. The measure gt-i begins at 17. A less or equal branch increments i; a greater branch decrements gt. Each iteration lowers this measure by one, so exactly 17 iterations occur. The pivot slot can receive a different key during a swap. Subsequent comparisons then use a changing threshold, whereas previously classified regions were proved relative to the original threshold. The equal block occupies ranks 13 through 32. Rank 40 continues in the greater region with rank 40−12−20=8, which is valid in a region of size 18. The classifier has linear work regardless of the requested rank. Question 43. Balanced selection versus balanced sorting

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

With a true median pivot costing linear work, compare recurrences for selecting one rank and sorting all keys. Explain the difference in total work.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Selection retains at most one half: T(n)≤T(n/2)+cn, whose level tolls sum to at most 2cn up to rounding. Sorting visits both halves: S(n)=2S(n/2)+cn, giving cn per level for Θ(logn) levels and total Θ(nlogn). Question 44. Expected cost is not an average-input promise

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Explain what maxAER[T(A,R)]=O(n) says about randomized selection. Does it exclude a quadratic execution on a fixed array?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

For every fixed valid array A, average the running time over the algorithm's random choices R, then take the worst such expectation among arrays of length n. This is a stronger input guarantee than an average over a chosen distribution of arrays. It does not bound each individual random sequence: repeatedly selecting an extreme pivot may still give quadratic work. Thus a fixed adversarially ordered input cannot force a bad expectation under conditional uniform random pivots, but bad luck can still produce a slow individual run.

Question 45. Expectation cannot be moved through a function

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Reconstructed CMU 15-451 Fall 2024, lecture 1 exercise 1

Give an increasing positive function and a positive random variable for which E[F(X)]>F(E[X]). Then create a family with a growing ratio.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Take F(x)=x2 and X∈{1,3} equally likely: E[F(X)]=5 while F(E[X])=4. For a growing ratio, let X=M2 with probability 1/M and 1 otherwise. Then E[X]=M+1−1/M, whose square is Θ(M2), while E[X2]=M3+1−1/M=Θ(M3). The ratio is Θ(M). This disproves the substitution in general; assuming selection's cost is linear before proving it would conceal the issue through circular reasoning.

Question 46. A phase proof with a different good-pivot probability

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Suppose every partition costs at most cm on active length m. A good pivot occurs with conditional probability at least 1/3 and leaves at most 2m/3. Bound expected total work by phases.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The expected number of partitions before a good pivot is at most three: the probability of more than t failures is at most (2/3)t, even with history-dependent choices satisfying the conditional bound. A phase starting at size M costs at most 3cM in expectation. Phase sizes form n,(2/3)n,(2/3)2n,…, so total expected work is at most 3cn/(1−2/3)=9cn, plus a bounded base cost. This proof bounds real work, rather than inserting an expected child size into an unknown nonlinear recurrence.

Question 47. Tail bound for unlucky pivots

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

In the good-pivot phase with conditional success probability at least 1/2, bound the probability that more than ten partitions occur before the phase ends. Does this alone imply an exponential tail for total running time?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The phase survives ten attempts only if each fails to finish it, so conditional multiplication gives probability at most 2−10=1/1024. No independence between full histories is needed when each conditional failure probability is at most one half. This bound concerns one phase. A whole-runtime tail requires combining phases and their different work weights, not simply substituting “ten” for the number of algorithm iterations. The expected linear proof follows by summing phase expectations, while a sharper concentration theorem needs another argument.

Question 48. Exact expected comparisons for three keys

Read the complete solution and reasoning

For two keys, selecting either rank always costs one comparison. For C(3,1), pivot ranks 1, 2 and 3 leave respectively no child, a one-key child and a two-key child. Their additional costs are 0, 0 and 1, so C(3,1)=2+1/3=7/3. For rank 2, pivot ranks 1 and 3 each leave a two-key rank query, while pivot rank 2 ends immediately; C(3,2)=2+2/3=8/3. These are averages over uniform pivot ranks, not Boolean-comparison costs of the duplicate-aware classifier.

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

With 200 keys grouped in fives, apply the conservative symmetric bound 3(⌈n/10⌉−2). What minimum number is certified on each weak side, and what is the maximum strict child length?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Here ⌈200/10⌉=20, so the certificate gives 3(20−2)=54 occurrences on each weak side. Any strict greater child excludes the certified at-most-pivot occurrences, and any strict less child excludes the certified at-least-pivot occurrences. Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

There are zero strictly smaller keys, so that claim is false. However all 200 keys are at most the pivot and all are at least it. The only feasible A count is i=0, so j=3. Conceptually AL=−∞ and AR=+∞, while BL=8 and BR=11. Both cross inequalities hold, and the left maximum is 8. No empty-array element is accessed. Numeric sentinels are convenient here, but general record comparators need symbolic missing-boundary handling. If both arrays were empty, rank 3 would fail validation rather than entering this search.

Two sorted arrays: feasible cross-boundary cuts

Green records form a left side of exactly k occurrences. The two cross inequalities certify that every left key is no larger than every right key.

The arrays remain fixed; only the feasible cut changes. A wrong cross inequality determines the search direction.

Question 64. Input medians do not determine union median

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Use A=[1,100,101] and B=[2,3,4] to refute averaging input medians as a union-median algorithm.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The two input medians are 100 and 3, whose average is 51.5. Their sorted union is [1,2,3,4,100,101], whose numerical median is (3+4)/2=3.5, and lower median is 3. Input medians describe only each array's internal middle; they reveal neither how many keys from one input lie around the other's middle nor their complete interleaving. Cross-boundary cuts use that missing information while retaining logarithmic search over the smaller array.

Question 65. Two-array cut interval size

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Arrays have lengths 5 and 1000. Compare feasible i counts for union ranks 3, 500 and 1004, and identify the search-size bound.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

For rank 3, i ranges from 0 to 3, giving four possible cuts. For rank 500, it ranges from 0 to 5, giving six cuts. For rank 1004, it ranges from 4 to 5, giving two cuts. These follow from max(0,k−n)≤i≤min(k,m). At most m+1=6 cuts exist, so iteration count is logarithmic in the smaller length plus one. Searching all 1005 output positions is unnecessary because sortedness reduces the feasible split parameter.

Question 66. Tight asymptotic two-array median bound

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Reconstructed CMU 15-451 Fall 2005, homework 2 problem 1

For two sorted distinct arrays of equal length n, derive tight asymptotic comparison bounds for their lower union median. Do not claim the displayed cut implementation is exactly comparison-optimal.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The cut algorithm searches at most n+1 split counts, using constant boundary comparisons per iteration, hence O(log(n+1)). Across valid interleavings the rank- n output can occupy any of 2n input locations. For an A location, choose a sufficient number of smaller B keys to fill rank n; symmetric constructions cover B. A binary comparison tree therefore needs at least ⌈log2(2n)⌉ depth. The asymptotic bound is Θ(logn). Constants and exact optimal counts need a more refined algorithm and decision-tree argument.

Question 67. Taking all threshold ties overproduces top-k

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Find exactly four smallest occurrences of [1,2,2,2,2,8] after selecting rank 4. How many threshold-equal occurrences must be included?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The selected value is 2. One occurrence is strictly smaller, so exactly 4−1=3 of the four occurrences equal to 2 must be retained. Taking every key at most 2 outputs five rather than four. If identities matter, choose those three according to a stated tie rule, such as original-order stability. Selecting a key threshold certifies the value but does not by itself specify which equal records belong in an exactly sized output.

Quickselect: discard the irrelevant strict region

Record identities move; zero-based slot labels do not. Green is less, purple equal, amber unknown and blue greater. The requested global index stays fixed.

The pivot value is saved. Only the active range is unknown; outside records were excluded by previous rank certificates.

Question 68. Sorted top-k cost

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

An unsorted array has n records, and its smallest k records must be output in sorted order. Explain an O(n+klogk) deterministic method and when it equals full sorting asymptotically.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Select the k th key in worst-case linear time, extract every smaller record and only enough equal records to reach k, then comparison-sort those k records. Selection and scanning cost O(n); output sorting costs O(klogk). For fixed k this is linear. For k=n, the term becomes O(nlogn), consistent with the full-sorting lower bound. Unsorted top-k needs no final sorting, while requiring sorted output for large k adds genuine information requirements.

Question 69. Streaming top-k root meaning

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

To retain the three largest values from [5,1,9,4,8,2], should the retained heap be a min-heap or max-heap? Trace its retained sets.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Use a min-heap because its root is the weakest retained value and the candidate for eviction. After the first three values the set is {1,5,9}. Arrival 4 replaces 1, giving {4,5,9}. Arrival 8 replaces 4, giving {5,8,9}. Arrival 2 is below the root and is discarded. A max-heap exposes the strongest retained value and cannot directly identify the record to evict. Maintaining a size-three heap uses bounded space; sorted final output is a separate step.

Question 70. Rank interval output

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Reconstructed CMU 15-451 Fall 2024, lecture 1 exercise 4

Given distinct keys and ranks i≤j, output exactly the keys with ranks in [i,j] in O(n) time, excluding any requested internal sorting.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Use deterministic selection to obtain boundary values u=x(i) and v=x(j), each in O(n) time. Scan the array and output keys satisfying u≤x≤v. Distinctness makes their number exactly j−i+1. Total work is linear plus output size, which is at most n. If duplicates are allowed, including all equal boundary keys can overproduce; add occurrence counts and a tie policy. If output must be sorted, sorting the retained interval adds its own comparison cost.

Question 71. Multiple quantiles instead of repeated full scans

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

There are q known requested ranks. Explain why a balanced recursion over requested ranks takes O(nlog(q+1)) rather than simply O(nq).

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Select the middle requested rank, partition, and pass only lower requested ranks to the lower region and higher requested ranks to the upper region. At any depth the regions are disjoint subsets of the original array, so their total selection/partition cost is O(n). Each branch contains at most about half the remaining requested ranks, giving O(log(q+1)) levels. Equal blocks can satisfy several requests immediately. Running a fresh whole-array selector separately for each rank ignores the shared partition certificates and gives the weaker O(nq) bound.

Question 72. Why all ranks recover the sorting lower bound

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Why can one order statistic be selected in linear time while answering every rank on distinct keys requires Ω(nlogn) comparisons?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

One rank can be certified without ordering unrelated pairs. Answering all ranks gives the complete sorted sequence, distinguishing all n! permutations of distinct input records. A binary comparison tree then requires depth at least log2(n!)=Ω(nlogn). There is no contradiction: the outputs contain different information. A proposed linear method that returns every distinct rank has implicitly solved comparison sorting, so some extra assumption such as a bounded integer universe or uncounted operations must be present.

Question 73. Weighted median differs from count median

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Keys are [1,4,9] with weights [1,7,2]. Find the unweighted median, lower weighted median and weighted absolute-error cost there.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The unweighted median is 4. Total weight is 10; cumulative weights are 1, 8 and 10, so the first key reaching threshold 5 is also 4. The weighted absolute-error cost is 1|4−1|+7|4−4|+2|4−9|=3+0+10=13. Although the two medians coincide here, the coincidence follows from the weight distribution, not from a general equivalence. Changing weights to [7,1,2] would make the lower weighted median 1 while the count median remains 4.

Weighted median: accumulate mass across equal keys

Bar widths represent weight, not occurrence count. The threshold is half the fixed total weight; equal-key mass is accumulated together.

The sorted display is a transparent cumulative-mass demonstration; it does not claim that sorting is needed by the linear weighted-selection algorithm.

Question 74. An exact-half weighted gap

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Keys are 2 and 10 with equal positive weights. Determine every real minimizer of weighted absolute error and the lower weighted-median convention.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Normalize each weight to one. For 2≤y≤10, the cost is (y−2)+(10−y)=8, constant. Outside that interval the cost increases as the point moves farther away. Thus every real y∈[2,10] minimizes it. The lower weighted median is 2, the first key whose cumulative weight reaches half the total. Returning 6 as a numerical midpoint is also a minimizer but is not the lower weighted-median output. Exact-half cases must not be treated as unique-optimum claims.

Question 75. Aggregating repeated weighted keys

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Keys are [1,5,5,8] with weights [2,2,3,3]. Locate the lower weighted median and verify both strict-side inequalities.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Total weight is 10 and threshold is 5. Equal key 5 has aggregate weight 5. Weight strictly below it is 2, and weight strictly above it is 3, both at most 5. The cumulative mass interval reaches from 2 to 7, so the threshold lies inside it and the lower weighted median is 5. Counting repeated key 5 as a single unit rather than adding its weights loses the mass certificate. Cardinality and weight are distinct quantities throughout the weighted selector.

Question 76. A slope proof of the weighted median

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Prove that a key with no more than half the total weight strictly on either side minimizes ∑iwi|y−xi|. Include the equality mass.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

At a candidate key v, keys below it contribute derivative +WL, keys above contribute −WR, and keys equal to it contribute the interval [−WE,WE]. The total subgradient interval is [WL−WR−WE,WL−WR+WE]. It contains zero exactly when WL≤W/2 and WR≤W/2. A sum of absolute-value functions with nonnegative weights is convex, so a zero subgradient certifies a global minimum. Ignoring the equality mass would incorrectly reject a heavy repeated key.

Question 77. A count-balanced pivot for weighted selection

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Why can deterministic linear weighted selection use an ordinary count-balanced pivot even when that pivot does not balance weight?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The final answer is determined by the cumulative weight threshold, so compute lower/equal/greater masses and continue in the region containing that threshold. Runtime is determined by how many records remain to be processed. A count-balanced pivot guarantees that either strict surviving region contains at most a fixed fraction of the records, regardless of its mass. Maintain the already discarded lower mass when moving right. Returning the count median immediately would be incorrect, but using it as a pivot gives a linear-time weighted search.

Question 78. A heavy low key breaks unweighted reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Keys [0,10,20,30,40] have weights [96,1,1,1,1]. Compare the count median and weighted median, and compute their absolute-error costs.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The count median is 20. Total weight is 100, and the first key alone crosses threshold 50, so the lower weighted median is 0. Its cost is 10+20+30+40=100. At 20 the heavy zero contributes 96·20=1920, while the other contributions are 10, 0, 10 and 20, totaling 1960. Count-centrality does not describe the objective's mass. This example also shows why numerical distance and weight matter in the optimization statement, even though pivot correctness uses rank regions.
