Question 79. A depth cutoff is not a linear-work budget

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

An “introselect” variant permits ⌊log2n⌋ nearly full scans before switching to deterministic linear selection. Does this guarantee worst-case O(n) total work?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

No. If each permitted scan leaves only one fewer key, the prefix cost is n+(n−1)+…+(n−Θ(logn))=Θ(nlogn). A later O(n) fallback cannot undo work already spent. A genuine linear hybrid can instead allow only a cumulative partition-work budget of Bn for a fixed constant B, then invoke a proven linear fallback on the residual range. Naming a depth limit or a familiar library strategy is insufficient; the proof must bound the total prefix toll.

Question 80. Direct addressing changes the model

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Select rank k among n integers in [0,U) by a histogram. Give time/space bounds and explain why the comparison model cannot assume this operation.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Allocate U counters, scan all keys to accumulate counts, then scan counters in key order until cumulative count reaches k. Time is O(n+U) and auxiliary memory is O(U). Each key is used directly as an address, a capability beyond pairwise order comparisons. For very large U the method may be worse than linear comparison selection, and original record identities need extra storage. Model-specific lower bounds are not contradicted when the set of permitted operations has changed.

Question 81. Range sums with two boundaries

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original; range-search pattern from Princeton §4.2

Keys are [1,3,3,8,10] with weights [2,4,5,1,7]. Use prefix sums to answer the closed interval query [3,8].

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The prefix array is P=[0,2,6,11,12,19]. Lower bound of 3 is index 1, and upper bound of 8 is index 4. The sum is P[4]−P[1]=12−2=10, including both occurrences of 3 and the one occurrence of 8. The prefix invariant says P[t] sums the first t records. Subtracting inclusive element indices rather than exclusive counts can omit an endpoint. Once sorting and prefixes are built, each query uses two logarithmic searches and constant arithmetic.

Question 82. Mutation invalidates a static search certificate

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

A sorted index stores references to records ordered by their current key. One record's key changes without repairing the order. Why can a later binary search fail even though its loop invariant code is unchanged?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The invariant's elimination step relies on every earlier key being no larger than a tested midpoint and every later key being no smaller. An untracked key change can put a target in a region that the midpoint test discards. The loop still follows its update rules, but their justification no longer holds. Use immutable keys, update the index whenever keys change, or rebuild/validate after mutations. Testing the search code on a previously sorted snapshot does not certify its behavior after external changes.

Question 83. Increasing record-copy cost

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Keys compare in constant time, but each record carries a payload of B bytes copied during every exchange. What happens to a linear key-operation bound? Give an implementation remedy.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

A linear number of swaps can require O(nB) byte-copy work, so O(n) key comparisons do not imply O(n) total time when B grows. Store and permute constant-size references or indices, keeping payloads separately; then exchanges return to constant-size operations under the RAM assumptions. Key comparison itself may also be nonconstant for long strings. Always state which primitive operations are unit cost, and distinguish comparison counts from actual data movement.

Question 84. A sample median for selection

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original; transfer from MSc CE 1405 Q59

A sample of 2⌊n⌋+1 distinct keys is sorted by insertion sort to choose its median. If a quickselector then keeps one strict side, derive a pessimistic large-child bound and explain why this is not median-of-medians.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Let s=⌊n⌋. The sample has at least s keys on each strict side of its median. The rest of the array can all lie on one side, so the larger strict child can have size n−s−1. Sorting the sample costs Θ(s2)=Θ(n) in its worst case, and partitioning costs linear work. A pessimistic selection recurrence is T(n)≤T(n−s−1)+cn plus base details. This pivot certifies only about n exclusions, not a constant fraction; no array of medians from disjoint fixed-size groups is recursively selected.

Question 85. A square-root-shrink recurrence

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Analyze the equality recurrence T(n)=T(n−⌊n⌋)+Θ(n) with a fixed positive base threshold. Why is it slower than geometric shrink?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The active square root decreases by a constant-order amount per step for large n, so reaching the base takes Θ(n) levels. Upper bound: at most that many tolls, each O(n), gives O(n3/2). Lower bound: while size remains between n/2 and n, each step removes at most n keys, so at least Θ(n) tolls of Ω(n) occur. Hence Θ(n3/2). A sublinear excluded count does not produce the geometric series needed for linear time.

Question 86. A changing group size is not constant work

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

Suppose median-of-medians groups have size b=⌈n⌉ and each group is sorted by insertion sort. Why cannot the fixed-group linear proof be copied unchanged?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

There are about n/b groups and each worst-case insertion sort costs Θ(b2). Group processing alone is Θ(nb)=Θ(n3/2), not linear. The fixed-odd-group recurrence assumed each group has constant size, making its sort constant work. Even if a larger group gives a useful discard fraction, the local toll has changed and dominates. Choosing a different group-median method could change that toll, but would require a new explicit recurrence rather than the old constant-group argument.

Question 87. An adversarial nonuniform pivot distribution

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

A selector chooses the minimum current key with probability 1−1/n2 and chooses a uniform key otherwise, for a fixed original size n. Can it claim the conditional-uniform expected linear proof?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

No: its pivot distribution is overwhelmingly concentrated at an extreme. When seeking the maximum, the event that every one of the first ⌊n/2⌋ pivots is minimum has probability at least 1−⌊n/2⌋/n2≥1−1/(2n) by a union bound. On that event, at least Θ(n) partitions each scan Θ(n) keys, so expected work is Ω(n2). The conditional good-pivot probability is not bounded below by a positive constant independent of n. The algorithm contains randomness, but that alone does not imply the randomized-selection guarantee.

Question 88. A sublinear sample cannot guarantee an exact median

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

A deterministic pivot rule inspects only s<n distinct keys and returns one inspected key without examining the rest. Can it certify the exact median for all inputs?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Generally it cannot. Keep the inspected order unchanged and place the uninspected keys all below the returned key in one completion and all above it in another. Its global rank can then differ by n−s, while the observed comparisons and chosen output are unchanged. For nontrivial median sizes, at least one completion can place the returned record outside the required middle rank. The rule may give a sample-rank certificate or a probabilistic estimate under a sampling model, but not an unconditional exact global-rank certificate.

Question 89. A mathematical proof versus finite verification

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original

A test suite checks selection on every array of length at most six over three possible keys. What does this establish, and what must still be proved?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

It exhaustively verifies that finite domain and can reveal duplicate, rank-translation and boundary errors within it. It does not cover larger sizes, arbitrary comparable keys, memory limits or every random-pivot history. A general proof still needs the partition invariant, decreasing active size and correct rank transformation; complexity needs its separate pivot guarantee and cost model. Finite verification is valuable independent evidence, especially for an executable laboratory, but it is not a literal guarantee on every future examination question or implementation environment.

Examination rules and diagnostic traps

Examination rules: complete conditions, formulas and traps

Rule 1

Define the answer before selecting a method. Membership, insertion position, one rank, sorted top-k and full sorting are different outputs. A complexity statement for one cannot silently answer another.

Rule 2

One-based rank converts to zero-based index by subtracting one. Rank k refers to sorted-array position k−1. Check the source's convention before copying its recurrence or branch condition.

Rule 3

Repeated keys occupy an interval of ranks. Value v is correct precisely when |L|<k≤|L|+|E|, where L contains strictly smaller occurrences and E contains equal occurrences. Distinct-value ranks require another contract.

Rule 4

Keys and identities are separate. Two equal keys can belong to different records. Stable identity selection needs a tie policy such as original index, even when value selection is already correct.

Rule 5

The lower median rank is ⌊(n+1)/2⌋. The upper median rank is ⌈(n+1)/2⌉. For odd length they coincide; for even length they are adjacent ranks.

Rule 6

A numerical even median may not be an input key. Averaging two middle values requires arithmetic. A comparison-only order-statistic routine returns an input key and does not automatically compute that average.

Rule 7

A partition-selected array need not be sorted. Its cross-boundary inequalities certify the selected rank. Internal side order remains unconstrained, so binary search over either side requires additional sorting.

Rule 8

A comparator must support consistent elimination. Intransitive order, NaN without an explicit ordering policy, or keys that mutate during execution can invalidate the partition and binary-search proofs.

Rule 9

Unsuccessful unsorted equality search costs n key tests. Every occurrence must be ruled out unless an external index or extra information narrows the possibilities.

Rule 10

Successful uniform linear search averages (n+1)/2 tests. This formula assumes one matching occurrence and a uniformly distributed successful position. Repeated matches or nonuniform positions change it.

Rule 11

Include the probability of failure in expected search cost. With success probability p and a unique uniform conditional position, expectation is p(n+1)/2+(1−p)n.

Rule 12

Order equality-search candidates by decreasing access probability when permitted. The adjacent-exchange argument minimizes ∑ipi. This optimization does not preserve an independent numeric sorting contract.

Rule 13

Wrong-code feedback is not an ordered comparison. Sorting candidate codes does not allow bisection unless the feedback reveals which ordered region contains the answer.

Rule 14

Identification and successful action have different terminal costs. After eliminating all but one candidate, its identity is known, but opening a lock may still require the final successful trial.

Rule 15

A sentinel removes loop bounds checks, not linear key-inspection work. Distinguish the sentinel occurrence from a real match and restore any overwritten input slot.

Rule 16

The unsorted minimum needs n−1 comparisons. Every nonminimum must acquire a comparison-loss certificate, and one comparison can newly eliminate at most one minimum candidate.

Rule 17

Lower bound returns the first key at least the target. It may return n, which is a valid insertion boundary but not a readable element index.

Rule 18

Upper bound returns the first key strictly greater than the target. Replace the lower-bound < target predicate by <= target; this changes the equality-side update deliberately.

Rule 19

Separate the unknown elements from the possible boundary. In the half-open loop the unknown elements lie in [lo,hi) while the possible boundary lies in [lo,hi].

Rule 20

A false lower-bound comparison discards the midpoint itself. If A[mid]<x, set lo=mid+1. Keeping lo=mid can fail to progress on a one-element interval.

Rule 21

A true lower-bound comparison retains the midpoint as a possible boundary. Set hi=mid because that index could be the first qualifying key. Using mid−1 under this contract can skip the answer.

Rule 22

Prove termination with an integer measure. Every update must strictly decrease hi−lo until it reaches zero. Correctly naming a side is insufficient if the bounds remain unchanged.

Rule 23

The exact worst-case lower-bound predicate count is ⌈log2(n+1)⌉. For n≥1 it also equals ⌊log2n⌋+1. A final membership equality check is additional.

Rule 24

Do not confuse worst-case and a supplied trace. A midpoint equality can end ordinary membership search in one probe. A first-occurrence search usually must continue to establish its boundary.

Rule 25

Guard the final membership access. Test index < length before comparing the returned key. Empty arrays and targets above the maximum expose this error immediately.

Rule 26

Frequency is upper bound minus lower bound. The subtraction counts occurrences, including every repeated target, because the corresponding equal range is half-open.

Rule 27

Strict predecessor is at lower-bound index minus one. Strict successor is at upper-bound index. Check for missing endpoints before reading these positions.

Rule 28

A closed numeric range uses an upper bound at its upper endpoint. For u≤v, its occurrence count is ub(v)−lb(u). Two lower bounds instead count [u,v).

Rule 29

Sortedness is a global precondition. Checking only visited midpoints cannot certify hidden skipped regions. Revalidating the entire array for each query adds Θ(n) work.

Rule 30

Use overflow-aware midpoint arithmetic for valid nonnegative fixed-width bounds. lo+(hi-lo)//2 avoids the sum overflow in (lo+hi)//2; arbitrary signed endpoints still need a range analysis.

Rule 31

Binary search by answer requires monotonicity of feasibility. Prove that increasing the candidate cannot change true back to false. An attractive numerical parameter alone is not that proof.

Rule 32

Include predicate evaluation cost. If one feasibility test scans n records, a logarithmic number of tests gives O(nlogR) work over a range of R candidates.

Rule 33

Threshold search can validly return “none.” In a false-then-true candidate interval [0,N), returned boundary N means no true candidate. It should not be confused with a feasible value inside the domain.

Rule 34

Unknown-bound search needs both doubling and bisection. With a finite first true index t, their combined test cost is O(log(t+1)). If truth never occurs, unrestricted doubling may not terminate.

Rule 35

Real bisection certifies interval width. After s halves the width is (b−a)/2s. A bound on the function residual requires extra assumptions, and floating-point stagnation needs detection.

Rule 36

Jump search trades block probes against local scans. Its simplified bound is n/b+b, minimized near n. Endpoint access must be constant-time for this to describe total operations.

Rule 37

Interpolation's expected doubly logarithmic behavior is conditional. Distribution, numeric arithmetic and progress assumptions matter. Skewed keys can make its worst-case work linear.

Rule 38

Count pointer steps when searching linked representations. Logarithmically many key comparisons can coexist with linear or worse traversal cost because a midpoint is not directly addressable.

Rule 39

The insertion-gap decision tree uses Boolean tests. Distinguishing n+1 gaps requires at least ⌈log2(n+1)⌉ such tests. A different observation primitive needs its own lower-bound argument.

Rule 40

Distinct rotated arrays expose a sorted half. Repeated equal endpoint/midpoint keys can hide the rotation and force linear worst-case membership work.

Rule 41

Strict bitonicity supplies a peak-search direction. An increasing middle adjacent pair sends the peak rightward; a decreasing pair sends it leftward. Plateaus require a revised contract and proof.

Rule 42

Pairwise minimum and maximum use ⌈3n/2⌉−2 comparisons for n≥2. Initialize an even input from one compared pair, and an odd input from one unpaired record.

Rule 43

Tournament runner-up candidates are only the champion's direct losers. A loser elsewhere has another larger nonchampion witness and cannot be the second-ranked distinct record.

Rule 44

A tournament's exact runner-up cost depends on its path. Total comparisons are n−1+d−1 if the champion played d matches. The balanced-bracket worst bound is n+⌈log2n⌉−2.

Rule 45

Second occurrence is not second distinct value. Repeated maxima can occupy both largest record ranks. Excluding all keys equal to the maximum is an extra requirement.

Rule 46

Keep a pivot key constant during partition. A moving record's original slot may receive another key. Saving the pivot value preserves the invariant's reference threshold.

Rule 47

Three-way partition maintains four regions while scanning. They are less, equal, unknown and greater. The final unknown region is empty; the equal region can contain many occurrences.

Rule 48

Reinspect the replacement after a greater exchange. Decreasing the right boundary classifies the outgoing greater key, but the incoming key at the scan cursor is still unknown.

Rule 49

The unknown-length measure decreases once per classification. Thus an active range of length m has exactly m classification iterations in the presented inclusive-pivot three-way loop.

Rule 50

A classification is not necessarily one Boolean comparison. The shown < then > code can use two predicates for a nonless key. Exact-count questions must declare their primitive convention.

Rule 51

A pivot from the active range guarantees a nonempty equal block. Arbitrary external pivot values can have zero equal occurrences, so a selector using them needs a separate progress argument.

Rule 52

Selection continues in one strict partition. Sorting continues in both. The pivot-computation recursion in deterministic selection is a separate representative-array call.

Rule 53

A rightward local rank subtracts both lower and equal counts. Its value is k−|L|−|E|. Subtracting one pivot is valid only for the explicitly distinct-key single-pivot contract.

Rule 54

Do not mix fixed global target indices with translated local ranks. Updating the global left boundary already accounts for discarded positions. Shifting the global target a second time changes the query.

Rule 55

All-equal input finishes in one three-way partition. A two-way implementation can have very different equal-key behavior and should not inherit this conclusion automatically.

Rule 56

Correctness and runtime are separate proofs. A valid extreme pivot can preserve rank correctness while causing nearly full scans repeatedly and quadratic work.

Rule 57

Distinct extreme-pivot maximum selection sums n(n−1)/2 pivot comparisons. This exact count assumes one comparison per nonpivot key, excludes pivot-choice work, and follows the explicit active-length sequence.

Rule 58

Conditional uniformity is the randomized guarantee's premise. Choose an occurrence uniformly from each current active range, conditional on the preceding history. Merely using a random number does not ensure that distribution.

Rule 59

Expected randomized cost applies to every fixed input. It averages over algorithmic randomness; it is not a promise that the input arrived in random order.

Rule 60

Expected linear work does not exclude quadratic unlucky runs. A worst-case bound over random choices is a different statement from a worst-input expected bound.

Rule 61

Never substitute T(E[X]) for E[T(X)] without justification. Nonlinear functions generally violate equality, and assuming linearity to prove linearity is circular.

Rule 62

Phase analysis bounds actual conditional work. A good pivot probability bounded below by a constant gives a bounded expected wait; constant-factor size reductions then yield a geometric expected-work sum.

Rule 63

Small-size rounding needs a real base case. The conservative randomized proof uses a finite base below eight and a 7/8 shrink bound above it. Ideal fractions alone need their rounding caveat.

Rule 64

Exact random-selection expectations condition on pivot rank. The recurrence has one appropriate child per pivot rank and zero child when the pivot itself answers the request. Its stated partition counter must match the question.

Rule 65

A median of medians is usually not the true input median. Its purpose is to certify enough exclusions for a pivot. The final answer still follows the requested-rank partition rule.

Rule 66

Count certified keys in disjoint original groups. A full group of five contributes three weak-side occurrences. Exclude problematic boundary groups before assigning a conservative finite guarantee.

Rule 67

Weak certificates are sufficient with duplicates. A strict greater child excludes every certified at-most-pivot occurrence; a strict less child excludes every certified at-least-pivot occurrence.

Rule 68

Include recursive representative selection in deterministic cost. The recurrence contains both T(⌈n/5⌉) and the one selected strict-child term, plus linear local work.

Rule 69

Unequal children do not fit the ordinary Master theorem. Use finite induction, a controlled recursion tree or a valid unequal-branch theorem with its assumptions checked.

Rule 70

The finite group-five induction must absorb additive constants. Child sizes sum to at most 0.9n+7; a fixed base through 140 and coefficient c≥20a give the stated linear proof.

Rule 71

Fixed odd group sizes above three give a subunit fraction sum. Their ideal sum is 3(b+1)/(4b). Group-sorting cost remains linear only while the size is fixed.

Rule 72

Groups of seven give ideal fractions 1/7 and 5/7. With toll exactly n, linear substitution needs coefficient at least seven; this is not an implementation's exact comparison constant.

Rule 73

A group-three recurrence bound is not a matching algorithm lower bound. The equality recurrence with linear toll is Θ(nlogn), while an algorithmic inequality establishes only the corresponding upper bound without an adversarial construction.

Rule 74

Repeated triple grouping changes the certificate. Two levels yield four original certified keys per representative and the ideal fractions 1/9 and 7/9, allowing linear analysis after boundary corrections.

Rule 75

Two-array selection searches feasible left counts. Use max(0,k−n)≤i≤min(k,m) and j=k−i. This prevents negative or oversized slices before comparing boundaries.

Rule 76

Cross-boundary inequalities for two sorted inputs are weak. Accept AL≤BR and BL≤AR. If AL>BR, decrease the A count; if BL>AR, increase it.

Rule 77

Exact top-k extraction must control threshold ties. Keep every strictly smaller key and only enough equal occurrences to reach k. Sorting the retained records adds O(klogk) to offline selection.

Rule 78

Weighted answers follow mass, not record count. Aggregate equality mass and carry the discarded-lower mass when moving right. Count-balanced pivots can still prove linear runtime.

Rule 79

A true linear hybrid limits cumulative prefix work. A logarithmic depth cutoff may already spend Θ(nlogn). A fixed Bn work budget plus a proved linear fallback supports a linear worst-case total.

Rule 80

Verification and preparation claims must have a stated scope. Finite exhaustive checks, authentic archive examples and course synthesis provide strong evidence within their bounds. They do not prove a literal guarantee of success on every unseen question; use the invariant, model and counterexamples to transfer the knowledge.

Editable exact-state laboratories

Each laboratory computes its trace from the submitted data. The animation follows the mathematical model of that algorithm: boundary elimination, moving record identities across three-way regions, grouped-median certificates, feasible cross-array cuts, or cumulative weight. Indices stay attached to positions while records can move. Step backward, seek, pause and restart allow inspection of every decision; reduced-motion mode preserves all states without animated travel. Invalid data leave the last valid trace intact.

Use 1–10 integers per array from −999 to 999. Boundary and two-array search require sorted inputs. Selection ranks must be in 1..input length or 1..combined length. Weighted mode needs one positive integer weight per key; it ignores the target/rank field. Group and tournament modes also ignore that field. The weighted model sorts for transparent mass visualization; the lesson separately proves the linear weighted algorithm. Deterministic demonstration uses base size five to expose small examples, while the finite proof uses base through 140. Invalid input preserves the previous valid model.

The chapter covers array searching and comparison-based order statistics, including repeated keys, weighted extensions and two sorted inputs. It does not claim an exhaustive survey of every specialized selection algorithm, every library implementation, or every historical examination. Formal proofs, source scope, independent finite checks and visual evidence are reported in the quality audit. The chapter remains a review draft until explicit student approval.
